items.title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
items.tldr: US midterm elections triggered a market rout that erased roughly $2.5 trillion in tech valuation, as Democrats won control of Congress and signaled tighter regulation of AI data centres. The sell‑off has revived concerns about an AI investment bubble and may reshape global AI policy, including the trajectory of agentic AI and large language models.
items.background: The 2026 US midterm elections saw Democrats capture both chambers of Congress, ending a decade of Republican dominance. Campaign rhetoric focused heavily on curbing the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, particularly the construction of data centres that power large‑scale models such as OpenAI's GPT‑4‑Turbo, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude. Prior to the vote, the tech‑heavy Nasdaq had surged on expectations that AI would drive the next wave of productivity, prompting record capital inflows into chipmakers, cloud providers, and AI‑focused startups. The election outcome introduced regulatory uncertainty at a time when billions of dollars were being allocated to build the physical backbone of generative AI.

analysis.heading: Market reaction and valuation shock
analysis.content: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, wiping out an estimated $2.5 trillion in market capitalisation. Nvidia, AMD, Micron, Intel and memory‑card maker SanDisk each posted double‑digit declines, while the broader S&P 500 and Dow Jones also slipped into correction territory. The rapid sell‑off reflects investors pricing in potential legislative constraints on data‑centre permits, higher compliance costs, and a possible slowdown in the rollout of next‑generation LLMs. The magnitude of the decline, the largest single‑day loss for the “magnificent seven” since 2025, suggests that market participants now view AI growth as more contingent on policy than on pure technological momentum.

analysis.heading: Regulatory thrust and the data‑centre moratorium
analysis.content: Democratic candidates campaigned on a platform of environmental stewardship and job protection, promising a moratorium on new AI data‑centre construction in several states, most notably Texas. Governor‑elect Gina Hinojosa's pledge to halt new facilities underscores a broader legislative push to embed environmental impact assessments, community consent mechanisms, and stricter zoning rules into AI infrastructure projects. If enacted, these measures could raise capital expenditures for cloud providers by 15‑20 %, delay the scaling of agentic AI systems, and shift competitive advantage toward firms that have already secured permits or that rely on more energy‑efficient hardware.

analysis.heading: Strategic implications for AI developers and open‑source ecosystems
analysis.content: OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic and other leading labs have built their most powerful models on massive data‑centre clusters. The regulatory climate may accelerate a strategic pivot toward open‑source model development and more efficient architectures, as companies seek to reduce reliance on costly, location‑bound infrastructure. Moreover, heightened scrutiny could spur the adoption of federated learning and edge‑AI solutions, which distribute computation away from centralized hubs. This shift aligns with growing policy interest in mitigating AI’s environmental footprint while preserving innovation pathways for agentic AI research.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical spillover: from the US to emerging markets like Myanmar
analysis.content: The US policy stance reverberates globally, influencing how other governments approach AI regulation. Myanmar, still grappling with limited digital infrastructure, watches the US debate closely as it contemplates its own nascent AI strategy. A US‑led regulatory template could encourage Myanmar to adopt precautionary measures that balance state control with the need for foreign investment in AI‑related hardware, potentially shaping the region’s AI talent pipeline and its integration into the broader LLM ecosystem.

key_facts: Nasdaq Composite down 5.5%, $2.5 trillion market‑cap loss.
Nvidia shares fell >9%; AMD, Micron >17%; Intel down 10.3%.
Democrats won control of US Senate and House, promising AI data‑centre moratoriums.
Tesla and SpaceX shares dropped 8%‑11%, shaving $300 billion off combined valuation.
implications: Higher regulatory costs could compress profit margins for chipmakers and cloud providers.
Investor confidence in AI as a growth engine may wane, prompting a re‑allocation toward more regulated sectors.
Policy‑driven delays in data‑centre construction could slow the rollout of next‑generation LLMs and agentic AI prototypes.
Open‑source AI initiatives may gain traction as firms seek cost‑effective alternatives to massive proprietary clusters.
items.outlook: In the medium term, the US Congress is expected to introduce a suite of bills targeting AI data‑centre siting, energy usage, and algorithmic transparency. If passed, these regulations could reshape capital allocation, favouring firms with existing infrastructure and prompting a wave of consolidation in the AI hardware market. Meanwhile, global competitors such as the EU and China are likely to accelerate their own regulatory frameworks, creating a fragmented landscape where compliance costs become a decisive competitive factor. Investors should monitor legislative timelines, the response of major AI labs to open‑source pressures, and emerging market strategies—particularly in regions like Myanmar—that may either adopt similar constraints or position themselves as low‑cost alternatives for AI compute.

items.fulltext:
Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in AI development.
Shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index closed down by more than 5.5% to lose an estimated $2.5tn (Â£1.9tn) in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of US President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

items.title: California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
items.tldr: Governor Gavin Newsom commuted all 548 death sentences to life without parole, citing moral, fiscal, and systemic failures of capital punishment. The move is both a symbolic rebuke of the death penalty and a pragmatic cost‑saving measure, while raising questions about the future of criminal‑justice policy and its intersection with emerging AI governance tools.
items.background: California has long held the nation’s largest death‑row population, yet it has not carried out an execution since 2006. The state’s capital‑punishment system has been plagued by legal challenges, wrongful convictions, and soaring litigation costs. Newsom, a Democratic leader of the most populous U.S. state, previously halted executions in 2019 and now uses his clemency authority to replace all death sentences with life without parole. The decision arrives amid a national resurgence of executions, heightened public debate over racial bias, and growing interest in AI‑driven risk analytics for parole and sentencing decisions.

analysis.heading: Legal and Constitutional Implications
analysis.content: Newsom’s commutation leverages the governor’s constitutional clemency power, a prerogative that bypasses the legislature and the courts. While the U.S. Supreme Court has upheld the death penalty as constitutional, the governor argues that California’s implementation is fundamentally flawed, violating due‑process guarantees through wrongful convictions and systemic racial disparities. Legal scholars note that the move does not abolish capital punishment outright—only the state legislature or voters can do that—but it effectively nullifies the death‑row pipeline, forcing the state to confront the ethical and procedural shortcomings highlighted by cases such as Keith Doolin, who maintains his innocence after decades on death row.

analysis.heading: Fiscal and Administrative Impact
analysis.content: The fiscal justification for the commutation is stark: each death‑penalty case can cost taxpayers upwards of $3‑$4 million when accounting for trials, appeals, and incarceration. By converting 548 sentences to life without parole, California could save an estimated $2 billion annually in legal and prison expenditures. Moreover, the state can redirect resources toward modernizing its criminal‑justice infrastructure, including AI‑enabled risk assessments that promise more consistent parole decisions and reduced recidivism. However, critics caution that the savings may be offset by the long‑term costs of housing inmates for life, especially as the prison system faces overcrowding and staffing shortages.

analysis.heading: Political and Geopolitical Ramifications
analysis.content: Politically, Newsom’s action reinforces his positioning as a progressive champion, potentially bolstering his standing among Democratic primary voters and enhancing his profile for a possible 2028 presidential bid. The decision also aligns with broader global trends toward penal reform, echoing movements in Europe and parts of Latin America that are phasing out capital punishment. In the geopolitical arena, the commutation underscores the United States’ internal divergence on criminal‑justice policy, a point of contention in diplomatic dialogues on human rights. Additionally, the move intersects with the editorial priority on agentic AI and LLM governance, as policymakers increasingly consider AI tools for sentencing risk analysis, raising questions about algorithmic bias and transparency in a post‑death‑penalty landscape.

key_facts: All 548 death‑row inmates in California had their sentences commuted to life without parole by Governor Gavin Newsom.
California has not executed an inmate since 2006, and only 13 executions have occurred since the death penalty was reinstated in 1978.
The commutation is expected to save the state an estimated $2 billion per year in legal and incarceration costs.
Newsom cited moral incompatibility with California’s values, systemic failures, and the risk of wrongful convictions as primary reasons.
The decision may influence upcoming midterm elections, with Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra projected to succeed Newsom.

AI companies such as OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic are increasingly involved in providing risk‑assessment tools for parole boards, a development that could be impacted by the shift away from capital punishment.
implications: Potential acceleration of AI‑driven parole and sentencing analytics as the state seeks more efficient and equitable justice mechanisms.
Increased political pressure on other states with large death‑row populations to reconsider their capital‑punishment policies.
Heightened debate over the role of executive clemency versus legislative action in shaping criminal‑justice reform.
Possible legal challenges from victims’ families and prosecutors seeking to restore death sentences through ballot initiatives.
items.outlook: The commutation marks a pivotal moment in California’s criminal‑justice trajectory, signaling a shift from punitive measures toward restorative and cost‑effective solutions. As the state embraces AI‑enabled risk analytics, it will need to balance technological innovation with robust oversight to avoid replicating historic biases. The political fallout will reverberate through the 2026 midterm elections and set a precedent for how other jurisdictions navigate the moral, fiscal, and technological dimensions of capital punishment. In the broader geopolitical context, the move reinforces a growing international consensus that state‑sanctioned killing is incompatible with modern human‑rights standards, while also prompting a re‑examination of how emerging AI tools can be ethically integrated into sentencing and parole decisions.

items.fulltext:
California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
- Published
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that FranÃ§ois Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.

items.title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
items.tldr: The Bank of England raised its benchmark rate to 4%, the first rise in more than three years, citing higher energy costs and the ongoing US‑Iran conflict. Policymakers warned the hike may not be the last, while households face higher mortgage repayments and savers see modest gains.
items.background: After a prolonged period of ultra‑low rates following the COVID‑19 pandemic, inflation in the UK has drifted above the Bank’s 2% target, driven largely by volatile energy prices linked to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The US‑Iran war has disrupted global oil supplies, feeding into UK consumer price growth. The Bank’s rate‑setting committee, meeting amid these pressures, concluded that a modest tightening was necessary to anchor inflation expectations without stifling an already fragile recovery.

analysis.heading: Monetary Policy Rationale
analysis.content: The Bank’s decision to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4% reflects a calibrated response to rising inflation, which hit 3.5% year‑on‑year in September 2026. Governor Andrew Bailey framed the move as a “one‑for‑now” insurance hike, emphasizing that it should not be interpreted as the start of an inevitable series of increases. However, he also warned that unless the US‑Iran conflict is resolved, further rate rises could be warranted. The committee’s vote was 8‑1 in favour, with the lone dissenter advocating a 4.25% rate, underscoring internal debate about the appropriate pace of tightening.

analysis.heading: Market and Household Impact
analysis.content: The immediate effect is felt most sharply by borrowers. Tracker mortgage holders—around 510,000 households—will see repayments rise by roughly £31 per month, while variable‑rate borrowers may face an additional £14 monthly cost for each 0.25 percentage‑point increase. Fixed‑rate borrowers remain insulated for the term of their contracts, but new products will likely incorporate higher margins. Savers benefit modestly, as deposit accounts begin to offer more attractive yields. The real‑world impact is already evident: a five‑year mortgage borrower in Brighton expects his monthly payment to jump from £1,420 to £1,680, prompting lifestyle adjustments such as cutting back on dining out and wine purchases.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Inflation Outlook
analysis.content: The Bank now projects inflation to peak at 4.9% in mid‑2027, well above its 2% target, and forecasts a return to target only by 2028. An “adverse scenario”—a further escalation of the US‑Iran war that drives oil prices higher—could push inflation to 6.2% in 2027. This outlook ties monetary policy tightly to external events, making the UK economy vulnerable to Middle‑East developments. The Bank’s forward guidance stresses that future rate decisions will hinge on the trajectory of energy prices, wage growth, and the broader inflation transmission to goods and services.

key_facts: Base interest rate raised from 3.75% to 4%, the first increase since August 2023.
Eight of nine MPC members voted for the rise; one member favoured 4.25%.
Inflation stood at 3.5% YoY in September 2026, driven by fuel and energy costs.
Bank expects inflation to peak at 4.9% in mid‑2027 and return to 2% only by 2028.
Tracker mortgage holders will see an average £31 monthly repayment increase.
implications: Higher borrowing costs may dampen consumer spending and slow economic growth.
Savers will see modest gains, potentially encouraging a shift from cash to other assets.
UK fiscal position could be strained if higher energy prices persist, limiting policy flexibility.
Financial markets will watch for signals on further tightening, affecting bond yields and equity valuations.
items.outlook: The Bank of England now stands at a crossroads where domestic monetary policy is increasingly intertwined with geopolitical risk. While the immediate rate hike is defensive, the outlook hinges on the resolution of the US‑Iran conflict and the trajectory of global energy markets. If tensions ease, inflation could moderate sooner, allowing the MPC to pause or even reverse course. Conversely, a protracted war scenario would likely force additional tightening, deepening the burden on households and businesses already coping with elevated living costs. Market participants will be vigilant for any shift in forward guidance, as the Bank’s credibility in anchoring expectations will be crucial to preventing a wage‑price spiral.

items.fulltext:
Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
- Published
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.
Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".
The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.
The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.
Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.
"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.
Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.
However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.
Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.
However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".
Inflation, which measures the pace of price rises over time, is well below its peak of a few years ago but remains above the Bank of England's 2% target and is expected to increase further next year.
Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September 2026, largely due to higher fuel prices. Millions of households are also set to be hit by energy bill increases in January.
Higher fuel prices can lead to prices rising for a host of goods and staples as businesses pass on higher costs to customers.
But the Bank said there was "limited evidence" this had happened so far for goods, such as food, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower margins.
In an interview with the BBC, Bailey defended the decision to raise rates despite the Bank's assessment that inflation was yet to spread to other parts of the economy.
He said further increases in energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and "that's what we have to seek to lean against".
Patrick Bryson, from Brighton, is set to see his five-year mortgage term with a 3.51% interest rate end soon.
The best deal the 51-year-old can find is a 5.17% loan with HSBC, which means his repayments will jump from Â£1,420 to Â£1,680 a month from February.
"The only thing that bugs me about the mortgage is that after five years of paying it off we are now paying more than we were before," said the father-of-three. "That's a bit of a slap in the face."
The guitar teacher, who has a combined income of around Â£68,000 a year with his wife, who manages a care home, said the couple is feeling pressure on their finances and so have changed their shopping habits and are looking to reduce their subcription outgoings.
"Over the last year I have stopped buying wine, we don't go out to eat much anymore, we have knocked takeaways on the head. The prices are ridiculous," he said.

The Bank now expects inflation to peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year, higher than it originally estimated, and not return to 2% until 2028.
But in an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it suggested.
While the UK cannot control global energy prices, the Bank raised rates, for the first time since August 2023, in order to limit the knock-on effects of high energy prices resulting in inflation going up across the board.
Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what customers for mortgages, loans, credit cards get charged, as well as savings rates.
The rate rise will see 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders see a Â£31 monthly jump in repayments, according to banking trade body UK Finance.
Homeowners on fixed deals will see no change, though future products may be affected.
However, people on variable deals will be impacted depending on how their lender reacts to the rate rise. Typically a 0.25pp rise means a Â£14 increase per month in repayments.
